questions.question: At the skate park near Ava's school, the ramp meets the flat ground at an angle of 145°. Which name describes this angle?
questions.explain: An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse, a straight angle is exactly 180°, and a reflex angle is more than 180°. The common trap is calling anything bigger than a square corner 'reflex' — reflex only begins past 180°.

questions.question: Maya opens her laptop until the screen and the keyboard form an angle that looks a little wider than a square corner. Without measuring, which is the best estimate for that angle?
questions.explain: Compare with the 90° benchmark: a little wider than a square corner means a little more than 90°, so about 100°. The common trap is picking 80°, which is a little narrower than a square corner, not wider.

questions.question: Malik places the centre of his protractor on the vertex and lines one arm up with the 0° mark on the inner scale. The other arm crosses the pair of marks labelled 60 and 120. The angle clearly opens less than a square corner. What is its measure?
questions.explain: Always read from the same scale that shows 0° on your base arm, then check the number against your estimate: an angle narrower than a square corner must be under 90°, so it is 60°. The common trap is reading the other scale and writing 120°.

questions.question: A four-sided flower bed at the community garden has two square corners of 90°, and a third angle of 65°. What is the size of the fourth angle?
questions.explain: The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, so 360° − 90° − 90° − 65° = 115°. The common trap is using 180° (the triangle rule) and answering 25°.

questions.question: Sam has no protractor and must estimate the angle between two roads at a Burnaby intersection. The angle opens clearly wider than a square corner but is still a bit less than a flat, straight line. Which estimate is best?
questions.explain: Use the 90° and 180° benchmarks: wider than 90° but not yet 180° puts the angle near 160°. The common trap is choosing 190°, which is past straight, or 85°, which is still narrower than a square corner.

questions.question: Priya wants to draw a 130° angle. She puts the protractor's centre on the vertex and lines her base arm up with the 0° on the outer scale, but then marks the 130 on the inner scale by mistake. What angle did she actually draw?
questions.explain: The two scales always add to 180°, so a mark at 130 on the wrong scale gives 180° − 130° = 50°. The common trap is trusting the number you marked; estimating first (130° should look wider than a square corner) catches the error right away.

questions.question: Ana is sewing a triangular pennant for her school team. The angle at the top point is 40°, and the two bottom angles are equal to each other. How big is each bottom angle?
questions.explain: First take the top angle away from 180°: 180° − 40° = 140°, then split that evenly between the two equal angles: 140° ÷ 2 = 70°. The common trap is stopping at 140° and forgetting that it belongs to two angles.

questions.question: A security camera at a Richmond mall turns through the reflex angle between two walls. Nadia measures the smaller opening between the two walls with her protractor and reads 130°. What is the size of the reflex angle the camera sweeps through?
questions.explain: The small angle and the reflex angle together make a full turn, so the reflex angle is 360° − 130° = 230°. The common trap is subtracting from 180° (giving 50°) or doubling the 130°, but a reflex angle must land between 180° and 360°.
